The Dirichlet-convolution identity and the constant-one function
Arithmetic functions form a commutative ring under pointwise addition and Dirichlet convolution
items.strategy: Use the field structure of C for pointwise addition. For convolution, reindex by d <-> n/d for commutativity, and reindex the triple sum over abc = n for associativity; distributivity and the epsilon identity are direct finite-sum manipulations.

items.title: An arithmetic function has a Dirichlet inverse exactly when its value at 1 is nonzero
items.strategy: Isolate the divisor d = n in the equation (f*g)(n) = epsilon(n). The n = 1 case forces g(1) = 1/f(1); for n > 1 the remaining terms involve only proper divisors, so strong induction determines one new value at a time and also proves uniqueness.

items.title: Dirichlet convolution preserves multiplicativity, and multiplicative inverses stay multiplicative
items.strategy: For coprime m and n, identify every divisor of mn uniquely as ab with a | m and b | n, then factor the divisor sum into a product of two sums. For inverses, apply the same divisor splitting to the recursion from the inverse criterion and induct on mn.

items.title: Multiplicative functions are determined by their prime-power values
items.strategy: Apply multiplicativity to the pairwise coprime prime-power factors in the canonical factorization of n. For the converse, define f on products by the prescribed prime-power data and use uniqueness of the canonical factorization to prove the definition is well posed and multiplicative.

items.title: The divisor-counting function tau
The power functions id_k and the divisor-power-sum functions sigma_k
Liouville's function
The von Mangoldt function
The divisor functions arise by Dirichlet convolution
items.strategy: Unpack the convolution definitions: summing 1 over the divisors gives tau, and summing d^k over the divisors gives sigma_k. Then check directly that 1 and id_k are multiplicative, invoke convolution stability, and read off the prime-power formulas from the divisors of p^a.

items.title: The divisor sum of von Mangoldt is the arithmetic-function logarithm
items.strategy: Write n = prod p_i^{e_i}. Among the divisors of n, only the prime powers p_i^j contribute to the sum of Lambda, so the divisor sum becomes sum_i e_i log p_i; repeated use of the logarithm product law then identifies this with log n.

items.title: Möbius inversion gives Lambda = mu * log
items.strategy: Apply the published classical Mobius inversion theorem to the identity 1 * Lambda = log from the preceding theorem and keep the already-published Mobius carrier rather than reproving inversion locally.

items.title: Möbius inversion gives the closed formula for the number of monic irreducibles over F_q
items.strategy: Start from the published divisor-sum identity sum_{d|n} d N_d(q) = q^n. Apply the published Mobius inversion theorem to the arithmetic functions n N_n(q) and q^n, then divide the resulting identity by n.

items.title: The convolution 1 * lambda detects perfect squares
items.strategy: Write each divisor of n = prod p_i^{e_i} as prod p_i^{j_i}, rewrite the divisor sum as a product of finite alternating sums in the exponents j_i, and evaluate each factor as 1 when e_i is even and 0 when e_i is odd.

title: Arithmetic Functions and Dirichlet Convolution — Examples

items.title: A Dirichlet-convolution table through 12
items.strategy: List the positive divisors of each n <= 12, compute (1 * 1)(n) term by term from those divisor groups, and compare the resulting column with tau(n).

items.title: Computing a Dirichlet inverse recursively
items.strategy: Apply the inverse criterion to the constant-one function, solve successively for the first few inverse values, and verify both convolution orders against epsilon.

items.title: Prime-power formulas for tau and sigma_k in concrete cases
items.strategy: Factor several integers, apply the local prime-power formulas for tau and sigma_k factor by factor, and compare with direct divisor lists.

items.title: Euler's totient as the convolution mu * id_1
items.strategy: Start from the published divisor-sum theorem sum_{d|n} phi(d) = n, apply the published Mobius inversion theorem, and rewrite the result as phi = mu * id_1 instead of depending on the older worked example.

items.title: Checking the von Mangoldt divisor-sum identity on sample integers
items.strategy: Evaluate Lambda on the divisors of a prime power and of a number with three distinct prime factors, sum the nonzero terms, and compare with log n.

items.title: Working out the square-indicator convolution for prime powers
items.strategy: Compute (1 * lambda)(p^e) = sum_{j=0}^e (-1)^j for even and odd e, then interpret the two answers as the square and nonsquare cases.

items.title: Tau is multiplicative but not completely multiplicative
items.strategy: Use the local divisor-function proposition to compare tau(4) = 3 with tau(2)^2 = 4, while keeping the coprime case multiplicativity intact.

items.title: The Mertens conjecture is false
items.strategy: State the historical claim |M(x)| < sqrt(x) for x > 1, record the Odlyzko-te Riele disproof as a sourced computational counterexample, and keep it explicitly non-load-bearing for this page's finite convolution development.
